1.pericope_label: But now thus saith the LORD that created thee, O Jacob... Fear not: for I have redeemed thee, I have called thee by thy name; thou art mine. When thou passest through the waters, I will be with thee... I will bring thy seed from the east, and gather thee from the west

schools.summary: Ellicott reads the opening as a deliberate contrast with the wrath of the preceding verse, and finds in the title more than the Maker of heaven and earth, since God created Israel as specially answering, like other created things, to an archetype in his own purpose; to call by name is everywhere, and pre-eminently in the East, the mark of an individualising tenderness, almost of a predestinating love which makes the name a witness of its purpose. He takes the waters and the fire as the two contrasted forms of elemental peril, used proverbially for every kind of danger; paints God, after the manner of men, as surrendering Egypt and other kingdoms to the arms of Cyrus as though they were a price paid for liberating the Jews of Babylon, with the historical fulfilment in the later Persian conquest of Egypt; and shows that even from the prophet's own standpoint the dispersion was wide enough for the summons to the four quarters, since the ten tribes were already in the cities of the Medes, the Babylonian exile had begun, others were beyond the rivers of Ethiopia, and Phoenician traders had carried sons of Judah to the western isles. In the call to north and south he hears an escort of honour given by the heathen nations to the returning exiles. Delitzsch notes only that a second causal particle introduces the ground of the promise which secures them against water and fire alike.

Gill rejects two identifications before offering his own: the prophecy is not concerning Cyrus and the redemption of the Jews by him, as some have thought, nor of Sennacherib and the deliverance from him, as a rabbi and his father interpreted it, but of the Christian church, which goes by the name of Jacob and Israel since the first churches consisted chiefly of Jews. On the waters he reports a scheme preserved by a father of the church, that the Jewish writers made the waters the Egyptians, the rivers the Babylonians, the fire the Macedonians and the flame the Romans, which he calls not amiss while preferring the afflictions of God's people in general; and on the preciousness of the saints he denies every ground of merit, since they are of the same mass and lump with others, are not precious in their own sight, and are much less so in the eyes of the world. Calvin leaves open whether a new discourse begins here, since the prophets did not separate their discourses into chapters in a way that lets us know what they spoke on any given day, but thinks it connected with what precedes as a moderating of the severity just used. He makes the promise a warning as much as a comfort, since the Lord has not redeemed his people that they might enjoy pleasures and luxuries or abandon themselves to ease and indolence, but that they should be prepared for enduring every kind of evil; excludes all personal worth from the clause about being precious, so that the people may not boast of having obtained anything by their own merit; and says the four quarters include the whole world, as is customary in all languages, though the prophet speaks more loftily than the lawgiver because he wished the people to view the event as if it had actually occurred.

Clarke opens with an outline of the whole: a prediction of the blessed period when God should gather the posterity of Abraham with tender care from their several dispersions in every quarter under heaven and bring them safely to their own land. On the ransom he takes the words of Sennacherib's invasion, when the king, just ready to fall upon Jerusalem, was providentially diverted and turned his arms against the Egyptians and their allies, but grants that there are reasonable objections to this and offers a more general sense, that God has often saved his people at the expense of other nations. He parses the three verbs of the seventh verse in turn: created, produced out of nothing; formed, given that particular shape best suited to his station in life; made, adapted to the accomplishment of God's counsels and designs; and notes that ten manuscripts and two versions read the words for my glory without the conjunction. Wesley glosses the created as made a people, and that in so miraculous a manner as if God had created them a second time; identifies the ransom with the diversion of the Assyrian king who had designed to revenge his father's disgrace upon the Jews; dates God's affection from the choosing of the people; and finds in the last verse the reason for the whole, that God will glorify his power and goodness and faithfulness in delivering those he has formed for himself.

Henry begins from the join, calling the connexion with the close of the previous chapter plain but very surprising. It was there said that Jacob and Israel would not walk in God's ways, and that when he corrected them for their disobedience they were stubborn and laid it not to heart; and one would think it should have followed that God would utterly abandon and destroy them, but the next words are, But now, fear not, O Jacob, I have redeemed thee, and thou art mine. Though many among them were untractable and incorrigible, God would continue his love and care for his people.

positions.view: Not Cyrus and the return, nor the deliverance from the Assyrian, but the Christian church.
The gathering of Abraham's posterity from every dispersion under heaven back to their own land.
The exiles, addressed with a hope of which they could not have formed the smallest conception.
Israel, created as specially answering to an archetype in God's own purpose.

debates.question: What are the waters and the fire?

positions.view: A scheme he reports without adopting makes them Egyptians, Babylonians, Macedonians and Romans; he prefers afflictions in general.
The two contrasted elemental perils, used proverbially for every kind of danger.
Not the content of the promise but its ground, introduced by a second causal particle.
A warning that redemption is for endurance, not for pleasures and luxuries or for ease and indolence.

debates.question: When was Egypt given as a ransom?

positions.view: At the Assyrian invasion, when the king was diverted from Jerusalem against Egypt and its allies.
At the Persian conquest, God surrendering kingdoms to Cyrus as the price of liberating the Jews of Babylon.
Whenever it was, it is cited as past experience confirming a present promise.

outliers.note: Reads the calling by name as an individualising tenderness verging on predestinating love, making the name itself a witness of God's purpose.
Declines to say whether a new discourse begins here, on the ground that the prophets left no record of what they spoke on any given day.

themes: But now thus saith the Lord that created thee, O Jacob, and he that formed thee, O Israel, Fear not: for I have redeemed thee, I have called thee by thy name; thou art mine.

When thou passest through the waters, I will be with thee; and through the rivers, they shall not overflow thee: when thou walkest through the fire, thou shalt not be burned; neither shall the flame kindle upon thee.
For I am the Lord thy God, the Holy One of Israel, thy Saviour: I gave Egypt for thy ransom, Ethiopia and Seba for thee.
Since thou wast precious in my sight, thou hast been honourable, and I have loved thee: therefore will I give men for thee, and people for thy life.
Fear not: for I am with thee: I will bring thy seed from the east, and gather thee from the west;
I will say to the north, Give up; and to the south, Keep not back: bring my sons from far, and my daughters from the ends of the earth;
Even every one that is called by my name: for I have created him for my glory, I have formed him; yea, I have made him.

8.pericope_label: Bring forth the blind people that have eyes, and the deaf that have ears. Let all the nations be gathered together... Ye are my witnesses, saith the LORD, and my servant whom I have chosen... I, even I, am the LORD; and beside me there is no saviour

schools.summary: Ellicott hears the command come abruptly, as from a divine voice, and calls it a reversed echo of the close of the previous chapter: there Israel saw but did not observe and had eyes yet was blind, while here the blind and deaf, meaning the heathen or the Israel that had fallen into heathenism, are spoken of as having capacities for sight and hearing which will one day be developed. He identifies the challenge as the one already made two chapters earlier, asking which of their gods has foretold the former things; takes the witnesses as collectively addressed under the title of the Lord's servant, their calling and election not cancelled and still capable of fulfilment, so that in the restoration they should be a living proof of the foresight granted to the prophets and therefore of the foreknowledge of him to whom past, present and future are as one; and notes that it was no heathen oracle or soothsayer that had foretold the restoration, the eternity of God implying his omnipotence. On the closing clause he gives the literal sense, who shall turn it back, as one of the numerous echoes from the book of Job. Delitzsch says the address closes by holding up once more the object and the warrant of faith.

Gill runs through the older applications of the summons, to the bringing of Israel out of Egypt, to the deliverance from Babylon, and to the casting of the Jews into outer darkness, and settles on a summons to the heathen uncalled. He has the nations gathered, if it could be, in an open court of judicature, that their whole strength might be united, the most cogent arguments any of them can produce might be brought out, and all might hear the cause fairly argued and judge for themselves; and he makes the witnesses both Israel, who could testify that God foretold their affliction in Egypt many hundreds of years before it came to pass, and the apostles and ministers and all Christian people, who are witnesses of the prophecies concerning Christ. Calvin finds the brevity of the eighth verse obscure, reports two renderings he does not take, that God will bring out both the blind and him who has eyes, and that the eyes meant are too dim to perceive the secrets of heavenly wisdom, and prefers on a careful survey to interpret the phrases separately, so that God brings out the blind in order to restore their sight and the deaf in order to restore their hearing. He warns how hard the argument is, since it is easy to ascribe to God the glory of divinity but very difficult to claim it so exclusively that all false gods are reduced to nothing, and notes that at the ruin of the nation unbelievers had applauded their gods as if they had vanquished the true God. God therefore separates himself from the multitude of them and produces his own witnesses, that he may not be thought of the same class, while indirectly reproaching those witnesses with ingratitude if they will not declare what they know; and in the eternity of God he finds the reminder that the world is his workmanship, since he who has a beginning and is not from himself cannot govern what he did not create.

Clarke understands the blind and deaf of the Gentiles rather than the Jews, arguing that their natural faculties, if they had made proper use of them, must have led them to the knowledge of the being and attributes of the one true God, whose eternal power and Godhead are clearly seen in his works, and would have preserved them from the folly and absurdity of worshipping idols. He notes a variant in the ninth verse, where seven manuscripts and two versions read who among you rather than who among them, though he thinks the received reading preferable; separates the two terms of the tenth verse, making the Israelites the witnesses and the prophet the servant whom God had chosen; and calls the clause about no God formed before or after a most difficult place, since there was no time when God was not and none when he will not be, answering that the words must be referred to creation, so that before me no god created anything, nor was anything pre-existent but myself. Wesley makes the summons a challenge to the idolatrous Gentiles to bring forth their false gods, which have eyes but see not; takes the servant for Cyrus, an eminent instance and proof of God's foreknowledge, or else for the Messiah, the most eminent witness in this cause; and reads the last clause as contempt, since the heathen gods neither had a being before God nor shall continue after him, and are called formed gods to show the ridiculousness of their pretence.

Henry stages the passage as a trial. God challenges the worshippers of idols to produce such proofs of the divinity of their false gods as this one instance, the redemption of the Jews out of Babylon, furnished the people of Israel with to prove that their God is the true and living God, and he only. The patrons of idolatry are called to appear and say what they have to say in defence of their idols; and since their gods have eyes and see not and ears and hear not, and those that make them and trust in them are like unto them, the prophet may fairly call the idolaters themselves blind people that have eyes and deaf people that have ears.

debates.question: Who are the blind and deaf summoned here?

positions.view: The heathen, or the Israel fallen into heathenism, with capacities that will one day be developed.
The Gentiles, whose natural faculties should have led them to the one true God.
The heathen uncalled, after several older applications are set aside.
The idolatrous Gentiles, told to bring forth the gods that have eyes but see not.
The idolaters themselves, who are like the idols they make.

debates.question: Who is the servant named beside the witnesses?

positions.view: The prophet, distinguished from the Israelites who are the witnesses.
Cyrus, an eminent proof of God's foreknowledge, or else the Messiah.
The whole people, collectively addressed under that title.
The witnesses God produces to distinguish himself from the multitude of idols.
Israel for the exodus and the apostles for the prophecies of Christ alike.

debates.question: What does before me there was no God formed mean?

positions.view: It must be referred to creation: before me no god created anything, nor was anything pre-existent but myself.
The heathen gods had no being before God nor shall continue after him; they are called formed gods in contempt.
God's eternity implies that the world is his workmanship, since one who has a beginning cannot govern what he did not create.
The object and warrant of faith, held up once more as the address closes.

outliers.note: Splits the opening clause into two separate promises, bringing out the blind in order to restore sight and the deaf in order to restore hearing, against both rival renderings he reports.
Records a manuscript variant reading who among you for who among them, then declines to adopt it.

themes: Bring forth the blind people that have eyes, and the deaf that have ears.

Let all the nations be gathered together, and let the people be assembled: who among them can declare this, and shew us former things? let them bring forth their witnesses, that they may be justified: or let them hear, and say, It is truth.

Ye are my witnesses, saith the Lord, and my servant whom I have chosen: that ye may know and believe me, and understand that I am he: before me there was no God formed, neither shall there be after me.
I, even I, am the Lord; and beside me there is no saviour.
I have declared, and have saved, and I have shewed, when there was no strange god among you: therefore ye are my witnesses, saith the Lord, that I am God.
Yea, before the day was I am he; and there is none that can deliver out of my hand: I will work, and who shall let it?

14.pericope_label: Thus saith the LORD, your redeemer, the Holy One of Israel; For your sake I have sent to Babylon... Remember ye not the former things, neither consider the things of old. Behold, I will do a new thing... This people have I formed for myself; they shall shew forth my praise

schools.summary: Ellicott notes that the place of exile is here named for the first time in this part of the book, would render the second clause I will bring them all down as fugitives, and takes the margin's bars for a variant reading, defences in the sense of defenders. On the ships he hears a deliberate irony, rendering the phrase into the ships of their shouting, that is, the ships which used to echo with the exulting joy of sailors, the word for shouting purposely chosen to suggest that a shout of another kind is coming, the wailing cry of despair. In the way through the sea he finds a distinct echo of the crossing narrative and of a psalm, so that the return from Babylon is a second exodus from another house of bondage in which, as in the first, the horse and his rider are thrown into the sea; and he glosses the quenching as that of a lamp-wick going out. Delitzsch marks a second field of the picture of redemption opening here, in which the words for your sake are expounded, and describes the road given through the sea and the path through tumultuous waters, the chariot and horse and army and hero that lie down together and never rise.

Gill takes the Redeemer for the one who redeemed Israel out of Egypt, would redeem the Jews from Babylon in a short time, and would be the author of a greater redemption than either, spiritual and eternal. He makes the argument from the sea practical, since he who made a way in the Red sea when he led Israel through it as on dry land could easily remove whatever difficulties lay in the way of this deliverance; and he takes the new thing for the incarnation of the Son of God rather than the return, which he will accept only as a type of the spiritual and eternal redemption. The beasts he refuses to read literally, taking them for the Gentiles, compared to such creatures for their savageness and stupidity. Calvin makes the conqueror a subordinate, since Cyrus will be but a hired soldier rendering his services to the Lord for the delivery of his people, and the prophet does not name him but speaks of the army under his command; and he observes that the words address not only those who beheld the accomplishment but all others whom God wished to comfort by a hope of which they could not have formed the smallest conception. He turns the recollection of former benefits into a duty, since we are ungrateful to God if they do not lead us to entertain hope for the future; explains that the miracles of the first redemption were of little importance beside the more remarkable one to come, whose glory throws the former into the shade as the brightness of the sun causes the stars to disappear, while insisting that the prophet does not mean the Jews should forget a benefit he had commanded them to publish in every age; defends the extravagance of the beasts' praise, since amidst so desperate a condition it was proper that magnificent language should extol the power of God, words supplying what seemed wanting in the reality; and closes on the ground of the whole, that they shall be saved because they cannot perish unless God's glory likewise perish.

Clarke supplies a commercial excursus on the ships. Babylon was very advantageously situated both for commerce and as a naval power, open to the Persian Gulf by the Euphrates, which was navigable by large vessels, and joined to the Tigris above the city by the canal called the Royal River, so that it drew the produce of the whole country to the north as far as the Euxine and Caspian seas; the queen who founded that part of the Babylonian greatness had improved the navigation of the river herself. On the new thing he keeps the reference historical, the same power that had been employed at the Red sea being employed again in their redemption and return from the Babylonish captivity, which was to be a new prodigy; and on the beasts he calls the image elegant and highly poetical, since God will give so abundant and miraculous a supply of water to his people traversing the dry desert that even the wild beasts, the serpents and the ostriches that haunt those arid regions, shall be sensible of the blessing and break forth into thanksgiving. Wesley says God has sent Cyrus against Babylon to this very end, that he might deliver them out of captivity, and takes the Chaldeans for the common people who make fearful outcries as they flee from the Persians in ships. He compares the quenching to the wick of a candle put into water; says that though the deliverance out of Egypt was glorious, yet beside the inestimable mercy of sending the Messiah all former deliverances are scarce worthy of remembrance; and observes that scripture often speaks of things at a great distance of time as if they were now at hand, to make us sensible of the inconsiderableness of time beside eternal things.

Henry explains the repetition. The faith and hope of God's people in Babylon were brought to so low an ebb that there needed line upon line to assure them they should be released out of their captivity, and therefore, that they might have strong consolation, the assurances of it are often repeated and here very expressly. God takes to himself such titles of honour as were encouraging to them, for he is the Lord their Redeemer, and will not only redeem them but take it upon him as his office and make it his business to do so.

positions.view: Cyrus, a hired soldier rendering services to the Lord, unnamed while his army is described.
Cyrus, sent to this very end, that he might deliver them out of captivity.
The question is answered by the title Redeemer, which covers Egypt, Babylon and a greater redemption than either.

debates.question: What are the former things that are not to be remembered?

positions.view: The exodus, thrown into the shade by a greater miracle, though the prophet does not mean it should be forgotten.
All former deliverances, scarce worthy of remembrance beside the mercy of sending the Messiah.
The return from Babylon itself, which he will take only as a type of the spiritual and eternal redemption.
The Red sea, whose same power is now employed again in the return, and that a new prodigy.

debates.question: What are the beasts that honour God?

positions.view: Literal desert animals, serpents and ostriches, made sensible of a miraculous supply of water.
The very beasts, impressed with a feeling of God's power, acknowledging and worshipping him.
Not literal at all, but the Gentiles, compared to such creatures for savageness and stupidity.
Creatures which would have cause to praise, if they had the abilities.

outliers.note: Interrupts the oracle for a survey of Babylonian navigation, its canal to the Tigris and its trade north to the Euxine and Caspian.
Reduces the conqueror to a hired soldier and points out that the prophet never names him, describing only the army under his command.

themes: Thus saith the Lord, your redeemer, the Holy One of Israel; For your sake I have sent to Babylon, and have brought down all their nobles, and the Chaldeans, whose cry is in the ships.
I am the Lord, your Holy One, the creator of Israel, your King.
Thus saith the Lord, which maketh a way in the sea, and a path in the mighty waters;
Which bringeth forth the chariot and horse, the army and the power; they shall lie down together, they shall not rise: they are extinct, they are quenched as tow.
Remember ye not the former things, neither consider the things of old.
Behold, I will do a new thing; now it shall spring forth; shall ye not know it? I will even make a way in the wilderness, and rivers in the desert.
The beast of the field shall honour me, the dragons and the owls: because I give waters in the wilderness, and rivers in the desert, to give drink to my people, my chosen.
This people have I formed for myself; they shall shew forth my praise.

22.pericope_label: But thou hast not called upon me, O Jacob; but thou hast been weary of me, O Israel... Thou hast bought me no sweet cane with money... but thou hast made me to serve with thy sins, thou hast wearied me with thine iniquities

schools.summary: Ellicott meets the critical question head on. The startling abruptness of the complaint, he says, has led many critics to question the genuineness of these verses, but their insertion by a later writer would be at least as hard to understand as their having come from the same hand as the glowing picture that precedes them. His own solution is that the prophet's experience taught him there would be in the future, as in the past, a dark side to the picture as well as a bright, that the mercies shown to the exiles would be measured not by their merits but by God's great goodness, and that the worship of the restored exiles would be as meagre and unthankful as the people's had been in his own time, visions of failure alternating with the hope that the ideal will be realised. He takes the clause about not being caused to serve as practically implying the suspension of sacrifices during the exile, since God had not imposed that bond service on them nor wearied them with demanding incense when they were far from the Temple to whose ritual it belonged; identifies the sweet cane as probably a species of spice used for the anointing oil and distinguished from the incense; and hears the verbs of the earlier verse repeated with the emphasis of scorn, the people having made their hypocritical worship a service which their God had to endure until he was altogether weary of it. Delitzsch prints the passage without comment.

Gill takes the failure to call upon God for a neglect of the whole worship, since invocation includes it, and notes that the Jews, though the posterity of a praying patriarch, did not tread in his steps. He keeps the sacrificial details literal, the small cattle being the kids and lambs which by law should have been brought for burnt offerings morning and evening, and the larger cattle brought still less, and reports that the versions give rams, sheep and lambs; these, he says, were not brought to God but to their idols, or at any rate not brought in a right way. On the sweet cane he has them think the calamus too expensive and leave it out of the composition, and reports two rabbis at odds, one holding they had no need to buy it since it grew plentifully in the land, the other answering better that it was not to be had there. Calvin raises the difficulty the passage creates: why should the prophet bring this reproach against the Jews, who were evidently very careful to offer sacrifices according to the injunction of the law? Some refer the words to the time of the captivity, when they could not have offered sacrifices though they had been willing, since it was not lawful to sacrifice in any place but Jerusalem; but he takes it rather as a general reproach. He adds that the name of God includes the whole of his worship, of which invocation is the chief part, so that a part is put for the whole, and that God elsewhere makes this plain by saying, after despising sacrifices and outward ceremonies, call upon me in the day of trouble. On the cane he gives God's own reply, that though they buy it with money they ought not to reckon that an expense bestowed on him, since they lost their pains in all those ceremonies by not looking to the proper end, exercising no faith and worshipping with no pure conscience.

Clarke answers the same difficulty by weight of emphasis. The Jews were diligent in performing the external services of religion, offering prayers, incense, sacrifices and oblations, but their prayers were not offered with faith and their oblations were made more frequently to their idols than to the God of their fathers; the emphasis of the sentence, on which the sense depends, is laid on the words me and on my account, and the Hebrew idiom excludes with a general negative, in a comparative sense, one of two objects opposed to one another, as in the saying, I will have mercy and not sacrifice. Wesley reads the not being wearied as a comparison rather than a chronology: God had not laid such heavy burdens upon them, nor required such costly offerings as might give them cause to be weary, nor such as idolaters did freely perform in the service of their idols. He allows two senses of the failure to honour God, either that they neglected sacrificing altogether or that they performed it merely out of custom and polluted their sacrifices by their wicked lives; and on the sweet cane he puts the reversal plainly, that they were niggardly in God's service while sparing no cost in the service of their idols, and had made him bear the load and burden of their sins.

Henry finds the charge doing two things at once. It comes in to clear God's justice in bringing them into captivity and to vindicate it, since it might be asked why the Lord dealt thus with his land when they were in covenant with him and had his sanctuary among them; and here is a good reason given, that they had neglected God and cast him off, and they must be brought to own this before they are prepared for deliverance. It comes in also to advance God's mercy in their deliverance and to make that appear the more glorious, since many things before observed magnify the power of God in it, but this magnifies his goodness, that he should do such great and kind things for a people who had behaved so.

positions.view: Many critics doubt them, but insertion by a later hand is as hard to understand as authorship by the same writer.
The charge belongs where it stands, since it clears God's justice in the captivity and magnifies his goodness in the deliverance.

debates.question: How can this reproach be true of a people careful to sacrifice?

positions.view: Some refer it to the captivity, when sacrifice was impossible; he takes it as a general reproach instead.
Their services were diligent but not offered in faith; the Hebrew negative is comparative, as in I will have mercy and not sacrifice.
Their offerings went to their idols, or at any rate were not brought in a right way.

debates.question: What does I have not caused thee to serve mean?

positions.view: The suspension of sacrifice during the exile, when they were far from the Temple to whose ritual incense belonged.
A comparison: God's burdens were lighter than what idolaters freely performed for their idols.
That the law's daily requirements were simply not met, whatever the versions call the animals.

outliers.note: Defends the passage's genuineness against critics who find its abruptness suspicious, arguing that alternating visions of failure and hope are characteristic of the prophet.
Rests the whole reproach on a comparative use of the Hebrew negative, so that the denial is of acceptable worship rather than of worship at all.

themes: But thou hast not called upon me, O Jacob; but thou hast been weary of me, O Israel.
Thou hast not brought me the small cattle of thy burnt offerings; neither hast thou honoured me with thy sacrifices. I have not caused thee to serve with an offering, nor wearied thee with incense.
Thou hast bought me no sweet cane with money, neither hast thou filled me with the fat of thy sacrifices: but thou hast made me to serve with thy sins, thou hast wearied me with thine iniquities.

25.pericope_label: I, even I, am he that blotteth out thy transgressions for mine own sake... Put me in remembrance: let us plead together... Thy first father hath sinned, and thy teachers have transgressed against me. Therefore I have profaned the princes of the sanctuary

schools.summary: Ellicott notes the same doubled pronoun in the first chapter, and offers the analogy as evidence of identity of authorship, since there too the incisive words that prove the guilt of Israel are followed by the fullest offer of pardon on repentance, and God does it for his own sake, to manifest the everlasting righteousness which is also the everlasting love, the blotting out finding an echo in an epistle. On the summons to remembrance he sets out two ways of supplying the object, either remind me, if thou canst, of thy merits and plead in thine own defence for an acquittal, or remind me of my promise to thee, of that electing grace which called thee to be my servant, and thinks the former fits better with what follows. He counts five interpretations of the first father, Adam, Abraham, Jacob, the ancestors of Israel collectively, and this or that high priest individually, and prefers Jacob; renders the teachers literally as interpreters or mediators, a term used elsewhere of ambassadors and standing here for the priests and prophets who ought officially to have been the expounders of the divine will; and takes the profaning of the holy princes to mean that in the exile their priestly functions were in abeyance and they were practically desecrated, the curse being the ban which answers to the anathema. Delitzsch makes the scene of the summons forensic, since justification is a legal act in which justice accuses and grace acquits, and asks whether Israel has any actual merits such that justice would be obliged to pronounce it just. He rules Adam out of the first father on principle, since Adam was the forefather of the human race and not of Israel and his debt was the debt of mankind, referring the words instead to Abraham as the first of the three from whom the origin and election of Israel were dated; and he rejects the future pointing which the old paraphrase introduced into the last verse, taking the holy princes for the hierarchs, the supreme spiritual rulers as distinguished from the temporal.

Gill reads the blotting out in allusion to the blotting of a debt book, since sins are debts, and these are many, and cannot be paid by the sinner. On the summons he denies that God ever forgets any of his promises, though he may sometimes seem to do so, and says he would have his people put him in mind of them that he may make a comfortable application of them. The first father he leaves undecided among Adam, in whom all have sinned and from whom all derive a corrupt nature; Abraham, the father of the nation, of whom they boasted and in whom they trusted, yet a sinful man though a great believer; Terah, who was an idolater; and some particular king, the father of his people. On the last verse he takes the princes of the sanctuary for the priests of the temple who had the care and government of things there, treated when the prophecy was fulfilled as common persons and divested of their office, their priesthood and its honour taken from them and the daily sacrifice made to cease. Calvin hears in the doubled pronoun a sharper rebuke of the ingratitude of men, who are wont to rob God of the honour that belongs to him alone, and takes the exclamation as a boast of his right to blot out the iniquities of a people who have no merits by which they could obtain it. On the summons he says that because the pride of men cannot easily be corrected the Lord pursues the argument and dwells upon it, to lead the Jews to throw away all confidence in their works, giving them liberty to say and argue whatever they please in support of their cause: if thou thinkest me forgetful, tell it thyself; remind me, if thou canst allege anything good; speak in thy turn, and I shall be silent. On the first father he reports that the passage is almost universally understood of Adam, that some prefer Abraham, and that a rabbi paraphrases the clause of Abraham's question how he should know that he would inherit, which Calvin remarks was not likely to occur to modern readers as the most striking proof that so eminently holy a man was not absolutely perfect; and on the last verse he prefers a future sense, applying it to the time of the captivity, while allowing that it may also be extended to the various calamities by which God had covered his people with disgrace.

Clarke finds the original of the opening extremely abrupt, three words meaning I, I, He, and asks whether there is any mystery in the form and whether it refers to a plurality of persons in the Godhead; on the clause for mine own sake he says that in the pardon of sin God can draw no reason but from his own infinite goodness. For the first father he quotes a rabbi with approval, asking how they can say they have not sinned when their first father Adam sinned and man has sin impressed on him through natural generation. On the last verse he emends the received text, reading with the Syriac and the Greek that thy princes have profaned my sanctuary rather than that God profaned the princes of the sanctuary, and prefers the singular of an ancient manuscript and three versions in the word for reproaches; and he closes with a lament of his own, that no national crimes have ever equalled those of the Jewish nation, since no nation ever had such privileges to neglect and despise. Wesley glosses briefly: it is God whom they have provoked who blots out their transgressions, and he does it not for their merits but of his own mere goodness; he remembers nothing by which they have deserved his favour; the first father may be put for their forefathers, so that as they were sinners so also were their progenitors, even the best of them; the teachers are the priests and prophets who were their intercessors with God, and if these were transgressors the people had no reason to fancy themselves innocent; and the princes profaned are the highest and best of their priests, given up to the curse, that is, to utter destruction.

debates.question: Who was the first father who sinned?

positions.view: Adam, on a rabbi's argument that man has sin impressed on him through natural generation.
Jacob, of five interpretations canvassed.
Abraham, since Adam was forefather of mankind and not of Israel, and his debt was mankind's.
Undecided among Adam, Abraham, Terah and some particular king.
The forefathers generally, since even the best of them were sinners.
Almost all understand Adam, though some prefer Abraham on a rabbinic paraphrase he finds unconvincing.

debates.question: What is God asking to be reminded of?

positions.view: Their merits, if they have any, so that they may plead in their own defence for an acquittal.
Any merit at all, in a forensic scene where justice accuses and grace acquits.
Anything good they can allege, God promising to be silent while they speak.
Nothing, since God remembers no desert of theirs.
His own promises, which he never forgets but may seem to.

debates.question: Who profaned whom in the closing verse?

positions.view: God profanes the princes, the past tense read as a future and applied to the coming captivity.
The princes profaned God's sanctuary; the received text should be emended from the versions.
The priests were practically desecrated, their functions in abeyance during the exile.
The hierarchs were profaned; the old paraphrase's future pointing is to be rejected.

outliers.note: Reverses subject and object in the last verse on the authority of the versions, so that the princes profane the sanctuary rather than God profaning the princes.
Excludes Adam from the first father on a point of scope: Adam's debt was the debt of mankind, and this verse is about Israel's.

themes: I, even I, am he that blotteth out thy transgressions for mine own sake, and will not remember thy sins.
Put me in remembrance: let us plead together: declare thou, that thou mayest be justified.
Thy first father hath sinned, and thy teachers have transgressed against me.
Therefore I have profaned the princes of the sanctuary, and have given Jacob to the curse, and Israel to reproaches.
